claim: The mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) encodes 13 protein-coding genes, each of which is a critical integral membrane subunit in the electron transport chain or ATP synthase.
source: Mitochondrial DNA serves as the template for the transcription of 13 protein-coding genes, each of which is a critical integral membrane subunit in the electron transport chain or ATP synthase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial genome composition and function.

claim: Several cancer types are depleted of mtDNA relative to adjacent-normal tissue.
source: In our own work (Reznik et al., 2016), we estimated mtDNA copy number for thousands of tumor samples sequenced by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) consortium and found that several cancer types appeared depleted of mtDNA relative to adjacent-normal tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Cells typically harbor an excess of mitochondrial respiratory capacity.
source: Respirometry experiments indicate that cells typically harbor an excess of mitochondrial respiratory capacity, implying that a modest decrease in ETC protein levels will not impact the basal respiration rate of the cell (Brand and Nicholls, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brand and Nicholls, 2011.

claim: A modest decrease in ETC protein levels will not impact the basal respiration rate of the cell.
source: Respirometry experiments indicate that cells typically harbor an excess of mitochondrial respiratory capacity, implying that a modest decrease in ETC protein levels will not impact the basal respiration rate of the cell (Brand and Nicholls, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of excess respiratory capacity, supported by citation.

claim: A sufficiently large reduction in the levels of mtDNA-encoded proteins will precipitate a drop in the rate of ATP generation via respiration.
source: However, a sufficiently large reduction in the levels of proteins encoded by mtDNA (e.g. large or complete mtDNA depletion), will precipitate a drop in the rate of ATP generation via respiration.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge of mitochondrial function.

claim: Cancer cells can partially compensate for lower respiratory ATP generation by increasing flux through glycolysis (the Warburg effect).
source: In these cases, cancer cells can partially compensate for lower respiratory ATP generation by increasing flux through glycolysis (i.e. the Warburg effect).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cancer metabolism and the Warburg effect.

claim: The majority of cancer types have lower levels of mtRNAs in tumors compared to normal tissue.
source: The majority of cancer types have a tendency for lower levels of mtRNAs, and five cancer types (breast, esophageal, head and neck, kidney clear cell, and liver) have lower levels of all 13 protein-coding mtRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: Five cancer types (breast, esophageal, head and neck, kidney clear cell, and liver) have lower levels of all 13 protein-coding mtRNAs.
source: The majority of cancer types have a tendency for lower levels of mtRNAs, and five cancer types (breast, esophageal, head and neck, kidney clear cell, and liver) have lower levels of all 13 protein-coding mtRNAs.
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Among the seven cancer types with statistically significant depletion of mtDNA content, all seven had lower mtRNA levels in at least 4/13 genes.
source: Among the seven cancer types with statistically significant depletion of mtDNA content in our earlier report (Reznik et al., 2016), all seven had lower mtRNA levels in at least 4/13 genes, with no mtRNAs showing over-expression in these tumor types.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of current data with prior study results, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: LUAD (lung adenocarcinoma) had lower expression of 6/13 mtRNAs despite being the only cancer type with increased mtDNA copy number.
source: We also observed that LUAD (lung adenocarcinoma), which we found to be the only cancer type with increased mtDNA copy number in Reznik et al. (2016), had lower expression of 6/13 mtRNAs, suggesting that any increase in mtDNA copy number in LUAD was compensated for at the transcriptional level.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2 and comparison with prior study.

claim: KICH (chromophobe renal cell carcinomas) had higher levels of mtRNAs in tumors compared to normal tissues.
source: Breaking the general trend, one cancer type, KICH (chromophobe renal cell carcinomas), had higher levels of mtRNAs in tumors compared to normal tissues.
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Each of the 13 mtDNA-encoded genes had greater than 2-fold over-expression in KICH tumors compared to normal tissue.
source: The over-expression phenotype was notably large: each of the 13 genes had greater than 2-fold over-expression in tumors compared to normal tissue (Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: KICH did not have appreciable accumulation of mtDNA copies in the prior study.
source: Importantly, KICH did not have appreciable accumulation of mtDNA copies in our prior study.
evidence: This refers to results from the prior study by Reznik et al., 2016.

claim: Eosinophilic chromophobe renal cell carcinomas have been proposed to arise from oncocytomas.
source: Eosinophilic KICH tumors have been proposed to arise from oncocytomas, a cancer type characterized by cytoplasms swollen with respiration-deficient mitochondria.
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the context.

claim: Oncocytomas are characterized by cytoplasms swollen with respiration-deficient mitochondria.
source: Eosinophilic KICH tumors have been proposed to arise from oncocytomas, a cancer type characterized by cytoplasms swollen with respiration-deficient mitochondria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about oncocytomas.

claim: The oncocytoma phenotype arises from somatic mtDNA mutations that render mitochondrial OXPHOS non-functional and defective mitophagy that prevents clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria.
source: This phenotype arises from two critical dysfunctions: somatic mtDNA mutations that render mitochondrial OXPHOS non-functional, and defective mitophagy that prevents clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria.
evidence: This is based on prior research about oncocytomas and chromophobe renal cell carcinomas.

claim: Oncocytoma cells experience an energy crisis due to defective mitochondria/OXPHOS and respond by further upregulating the biogenesis of defective mitochondria.
source: Thus, it has been proposed that oncocytoma cells experience an energy crisis due to defective mitochondria/OXPHOS (perhaps sensed through AMPK), and respond by further upregulating the biogenesis of defective mitochondria (Zong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zong et al., 2016.

claim: The increased mtRNA levels in KICH tumors likely reflect a drop in respiration.
source: Thus, our observation of increased mtRNA levels in KICH tumors is likely to counterintuitively reflect a drop in respiration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biology of oncocytomas and chromophobe renal cell carcinomas.

claim: The mitochondrial genome is transcribed in a polycistronic fashion, with all mRNAs and tRNAs on a strand transcribed simultaneously.
source: The mitochondrial genome is transcribed in a polycistronic fashion, with all mRNAs and tRNAs on a strand transcribed simultaneously.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial transcription.

claim: Following transcription, tRNAs are excised from the mitochondrial transcript, and the majority of the remaining mRNAs are polyadenylated.
source: Following transcription, tRNAs are excised from the transcript, and the majority of the remaining mRNAs are polyadenylated (Pagliarini et al., 2008; Mercer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pagliarini et al., 2008 and Mercer et al., 2011.

claim: Polycistronic transcription ensures that mtRNAs are highly co-expressed.
source: Polycistronic transcription ensures that mtRNAs are highly co-expressed, although it is clear from many studies that mtRNAs undergo a large degree of post-transcriptional regulation, resulting in uneven steady-state abundances (Rorbach and Minczuk, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the mechanism of polycistronic transcription, supported by citation.

claim: mtRNAs undergo a large degree of post-transcriptional regulation, resulting in uneven steady-state abundances.
source: Polycistronic transcription ensures that mtRNAs are highly co-expressed, although it is clear from many studies that mtRNAs undergo a large degree of post-transcriptional regulation, resulting in uneven steady-state abundances (Rorbach and Minczuk, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rorbach and Minczuk, 2012.

claim: Most genes encoding subunits of Complex I were downregulated in the majority of cancer types.
source: With regard to differential expression, most of the genes encoding subunits of Complex I were downregulated in the majority of cancer types.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Genes encoding subunits of Complex V (ATP6 and ATP8) and Complex IV (MT-CO1, MT-CO2, MT-CO3) were generally under-expressed only in the strongly mtDNA- and mtRNA-depleted cancer types.
source: In contrast, genes encoding subunits of Complex V (ATP6 and ATP8) and to a lesser extent Complex IV (MT-CO1,MT-CO2,MT-CO3) were generally under-expressed in only the strongly mtDNA- and mtRNA-depleted cancer types.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Papillary renal cell carcinoma (KIRP), esophageal carcinoma (ESCA), and thyroid cancer (THCA) showed an association between high mtRNA expression and increased age.
source: Among these, papillary renal cell carcinoma (KIRP), esophageal carcinoma (ESCA), and thyroid cancer (THCA) showed an association between high mtRNA expression and increased age.
evidence: This is supported by clinical association analysis using TCGA data.

claim: Five cancer types (ACC, KICH, LGG, PAAD, and LIHC) showed an association between higher mtRNA expression levels and increased overall survival.
source: More interestingly, we identified five cancer types (ACC,KICH,LGG,PAAD, and LIHC) in which higher mtRNA expression levels were associated with increased overall survival.
evidence: This is supported by Cox regression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Three cancer types (ACC, KICH, and LGG) showed associations between high mtDNA copy number and better overall survival in the prior analysis.
source: Three of these cancer types (ACC,KICH, and LGG), showed similar associations in our prior analysis using mtDNA copy number (i.e. high mtDNA copy number was associated with better overall survival (Reznik et al., 2016).
evidence: This refers to results from the prior study by Reznik et al., 2016.

claim: KIRP tumors showed an association between higher mtRNA expression and less aggressive disease, as assessed by pathological stage.
source: KIRP tumors also showed an association between higher mtRNA expression and less aggressive disease, as assessed by pathological stage (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by clinical association analysis.

claim: Down-regulation of nuclear-DNA-encoded mitochondrial transcripts is associated with poor clinical outcome across many cancer types.
source: Interestingly, these results echo similar findings by reported by Gaude and Frezza, who reported an association between down-regulation of nuclear-DNA-encoded mitochondrial transcripts and poor clinical outcome across many cancer types (Gaude and Frezza, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gaude and Frezza, 2016.

claim: Seven of eighteen tumor types had strong positive correlation between mtDNA copy number and mtRNA expression across all or nearly all mtDNA-encoded genes.
source: Seven of eighteen tumor types (adrenocortical, breast, glioma, kidney clear cell, kidney papillary, liver, and thyroid) had strong (BH-corrected p-value <10−5) positive correlation across all or nearly all mtDNA-encoded genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Seven cancer types had weak but statistically significant correlation between mtDNA copy number and mtRNA expression.
source: Seven cancer types (bladder, colon, glioblastoma, head and neck, kidney chromophobe, lung adenocarcinoma, and stomach) had weak but still statistically significant correlation.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four cancer types (endometrial, esophagus, pancreatic, prostate) showed no statistically significant correlation between mtDNA copy number and mtRNA expression.
source: The remaining four cancer types (endometrial, esophagus, pancreatic, prostate) showed no statistically significant correlation.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Of the seven cancer types with mtDNA depletion in tumors relative to normal tissue, five showed positive correlation between mtDNA copy number and expression.
source: Of the seven cancer types with mtDNA depletion in tumors relative to normal tissue, five (all but esophageal and head and neck) showed positive correlation between mtDNA copy number and expression.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and comparison with prior study results.

claim: Some genes (e.g. MT-ND5 and MT-ND6) had recurrently weaker correlation with mtDNA copy number, which may result from their lower abundance compared to other MT transcripts.
source: Some genes (e.g. MT-ND5 and MT-ND6) had recurrently weaker correlation with mtDNA copy number, which may result from their lower (and thus potentially noiser) abundance compared to other MT transcripts.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed data patterns in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: KICH tumor and normal samples had strong but distinct patterns of correlation between mtDNA copy number and mtRNA levels.
source: Upon closer examination of samples from KICH (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), we found that tumor and normal samples had strong but distinct patterns of correlation between mtDNA copy number and mtRNA levels.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: KICH tumors had higher values of the steady-state mtRNA/mtDNA ratio compared to normal tissue.
source: In particular, because KICH tumors only had increased mtRNA levels compared to normals (and not an increase in mtDNA copy number), the best-fit trend line between mtDNA and mtRNA appears shifted vertically when comparing tumor to normal tissue samples. Put another way, it appears as if KICH tumors had higher values of the steady-state mtRNA/mtDNA ratio.
evidence: This is an inference from data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Compensation for mitochondrial dysfunction in KICH may be via transcriptional mechanisms, rather than changes to mtDNA ploidy.
source: Given that many KICH tumors harbor mtDNA mutations, these observations suggest that compensation for such mitochondrial dysfunction in KICH may be via transcriptional mechanisms, rather than changes to mtDNA ploidy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns in KICH tumors.

claim: The mitochondrial genome encodes 13 polypeptides which serve as integral membrane subunits for 3 components of the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
source: The mitochondrial genome encodes 13 polypeptides which serve as integral membrane subunits for 3 components of the electron transport chain and ATP synthase (herein referred to as mtOXPHOS proteins).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial genome composition.

claim: The protein levels of mtOXPHOS and nuOXPHOS subunits must be coordinated in order to maintain proper stoichiometry of OXPHOS complexes.
source: The protein levels of these subunits must be coordinated in order to maintain proper stoichoimetry of OXPHOS complexes (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2013.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, the primary mode of regulation of mtOXPHOS and nuOXPHOS protein levels is through rapid translational, rather than transcriptional, synchronization.
source: Intriguingly, a study of the coordination of mtOXPHOS and nuOXPHOS protein levels in S. cerevisae found that the primary mode of regulation was through rapid translational, rather than transcriptional, synchronization (Couvillion et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Couvillion et al., 2016.

claim: In 9/13 cancer types, there was agreement in differential expression scores between mtOXPHOS and nuOXPHOS subunits.
source: In 9/13 cancer types, we observed agreement in DE scores between mtOXPHOS and nuOXPHOS subunits (e.g. see volcano plot of KIRC in (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Four cancer types (BLCA, BRCA, LUAD, and UCEC) have opposite patterns of differential expression in mtOXPHOS and nuOXPHOS genes.
source: More interestingly, we found that four cancer types (BLCA, BRCA, LUAD, and UCEC) have opposite patterns of differential expression in mtOXPHOS and nuOXPHOS genes.
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In BRCA, nearly all mtOXPHOS genes are down-regulated in tumors compared to normal tissue, while nearly all nuOXPHOS genes had increased mRNA levels.
source: For example, in BRCA, while nearly all mtOXPHOS genes are down-regulated in tumors compared to normal tissue (mirroring the mtDNA copy number depletion in BRCA), nearly all nuOXPHOS genes actually had increased mRNA levels.
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: For a functional electron transport chain, subunits of each OXPHOS complex must assemble with compatible stoichiometries in a process that requires coordination of individual subunit protein levels.
source: For a functional electron transport chain, subunits of each OXPHOS complex must assemble with compatible stoichiometries in a process that requires coordination of individual subunit protein levels (Mouchiroud et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mouchiroud et al., 2013.

claim: Treatment of differentiated C2C12 murine myotubes with certain drugs (including eukaryotic translation inhibitors) induced anti-correlated changes in nuOXPHOS and mtOXPHOS genes.
source: One report by Wagner, Kitami, and colleagues found that treatment of differentiated C2C12 murine myotubes with certain drugs (including eukaryotic translation inhibitors) induced anti-correlated changes in nuOXPHOS and mtOXPHOS genes, respectively (Wagner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wagner et al., 2008.

claim: The sudden shift of S. cerevisiae to a non-fermentable carbon source led to rapid induction of transcriptional changes in nuOXPHOS, but not mtOXPHOS.
source: Separately, Couvillion and colleagues reported that the sudden shift of S. cerevisae to a non-fermentable carbon source led to rapid induction of transcriptional changes in nuOXPHOS, but not mtOXPHOS.
evidence: This is supported by citation to work by Couvillion and colleagues.

claim: Rapid redistribution of mitochondrial ribosomes supported fast adaptation to respiration in S. cerevisiae.
source: Instead, rapid redistribution of mitochondrial ribosomes supported fast adapation to respiration (e.g. via an increase in translation efficiency of Complexes III and IV).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work by Couvillion and colleagues.

claim: Five cancer types (kidney clear cell, kidney papillary, head and neck squamous cell, liver, and esophageal) were mtDNA-depleted, under-expressed mtRNAs, and under-expressed nuOXPHOS genes, in comparison to normal tissue.
source: Five cancer types (kidney clear cell, kidney papillary, head and neck squamous cell, liver, and esophageal) were mtDNA-depleted, under-expressed mtRNAs, and under-expressed nuOXPHOS genes, in comparison to normal tissue.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple analyses in the study.

claim: A drop in the protein expression of mtDNA-encoded OXPHOS subunits will not necessarily precipitate a drop in respiration unless it is sufficiently large.
source: Importantly, because cells harbor excess respiratory capacity, a drop in the protein expression of mtDNA-encoded OXPHOS subunits will not necessarily precipitate a drop in respiration unless it is sufficiently large.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge of excess respiratory capacity.

claim: Clear-cell renal cell carcinomas are driven by homozygous loss of VHL, which leads to activation of hypoxia inducible factor (HIF), and subsequently increased transcription of glycolytic enzymes.
source: For example, clear-cell renal cell carcinomas are driven by homozygous loss of VHL, which leads to activation of hypoxia inducible factor (HIF), and subsequently increased transcription of glycolytic enzymes (Creighton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Creighton et al., 2013.

claim: The signature of HIF activation is evident in gene expression data and metabolomic measurements of KIRC tumors.
source: The signature of HIF activation is evident not only in gene expression data, but also in metabolomic measurements of KIRC tumors (Hakimi et al., 2016), and suggests that KIRC tumors experience a drop in respiration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hakimi et al., 2016.

claim: KIRC tumors exhibit increased levels (compared to normal tissue) of metabolites upstream of SDH (succinate dehydrogenase, Complex II), i.e. citrate, cis-aconitate, and succinate, and decreased levels of metabolites downstream of SDH (fumarate and malate).
source: In particular, KIRC tumors exhibit increased levels (compared to normal tissue) of metabolites upstream of SDH (succinate dehydrogenase, Complex II), i.e. citrate, cis-aconitate, and succinate, and decreased levels of metabolites downstream of SDH (fumarate and malate).
evidence: This is supported by citation to metabolomic data from Hakimi et al., 2016.

claim: The partitioning of changes in metabolite levels in KIRC could arise by a decrease in the activity of the electron transport chain and SDH, which would induce a metabolic bottleneck and the accumulation (depletion) of metabolites upstream (downstream) of SDH.
source: This partitioning of changes in metabolite levels could arise by a decrease in the activity of the electron transport chain and SDH, which would induce a metabolic bottleneck and the accumulation (depletion) of metabolites upstream (downstream) of SDH.
evidence: This is an inference based on metabolomic data patterns.

claim: Aspartate biosynthesis is heavily reliant on electron acceptors produced by mitochondrial respiration, and respiration-deficient cells become limited by the availability of aspartate.
source: In some cases, respiration may be critical to these processes; for example, aspartate biosynthesis is heavily reliant on electron acceptors produced by mitochondrial respiration, and respiration-deficient cells become limited by the availability of aspartate (Birsoy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Birsoy et al., 2015.

claim: Cytosolic acetyl-CoA utilized for lipogenesis is produced from the action of ATP-citrate lyase on mitochondrial citrate.
source: Beyond the ETC, cytosolic acetyl-CoA utilized for lipogenesis is produced from the action of ATP-citrate lyase on mitochondrial citrate, and substantial evidence supports the critical role of mitochondrial metabolism in producing adequate one-carbon precursors for nucleotide biosynthesis (Ahn and Metallo, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahn and Metallo, 2015.

claim: Mitochondrial metabolism plays a critical role in producing adequate one-carbon precursors for nucleotide biosynthesis.
source: Beyond the ETC, cytosolic acetyl-CoA utilized for lipogenesis is produced from the action of ATP-citrate lyase on mitochondrial citrate, and substantial evidence supports the critical role of mitochondrial metabolism in producing adequate one-carbon precursors for nucleotide biosynthesis (Ahn and Metallo, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahn and Metallo, 2015.

claim: Lung adenocarcinomas were the only cancer type to accumulate mtDNA copies compared to normal tissue.
source: To highlight a single example, lung adenocarcinomas were the only cancer type to accumulate mtDNA copies compared to normal tissue.
evidence: This refers to results from the prior study by Reznik et al., 2016.

claim: Lung adenocarcinomas had lower mtRNA levels of 6/13 MT genes using mtRNA data.
source: Using mtRNA data, however, these tumors had lower mtRNA levels of 6/13 MT genes.
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis in the current study.

claim: Mitonuclear protein imbalance in C. elegans promotes longevity via activation of the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRMT).
source: Prior studies of mitochondrial-nuclear (mitonuclear) protein imbalance in C. elegans claimed that it promotes longevity via activation of the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRMT), a transcriptional response preserving mitochondrial function in the face of stress (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2013.

claim: Activation of the UPRMT promotes tolerance of mutant mtDNA levels by activating mitochondrial biogenesis in an effort to recover OXPHOS activity.
source: Intriguingly, two recent studies reported activation of the UPRMT counterintuitively promoted tolerance of mutant mtDNA levels by activating mitochondrial biogenesis in an effort to recover OXPHOS activity (Lin et al., 2016; Gitschlag et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2016 and Gitschlag et al., 2016.

claim: The physiology and molecular constitution of mitochondria varies substantially from one tissue to the next.
source: It is well-appreciated that the physiology and molecular constitution (Fernández-Vizarra et al., 2011; Calvo and Mootha, 2010) of mitochondria varies substantially from one tissue to the next.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernández-Vizarra et al., 2011 and Calvo and Mootha, 2010.

claim: Across all tissues, mtRNAs were highly transcribed.
source: Across all tissues, mtRNAs were highly transcribed.
evidence: This is a general observation from the expression data.

claim: Substantial differences in the abundance of any given mitochondrial transcript were observed from one tissue to the next.
source: However, we observed substantial differences in the abundance of any given mitochondrial (MT) transcript from one tissue to the next (as evaluated using TPM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Samples derived from the kidney (TCGA studies KICH, KIRC, and KIRP) had exceptionally high levels of mtRNAs compared to other tissues.
source: For example, compared to other tissues, samples derived from the kidney (TCGA studies KICH, KIRC, and KIRP, see Materials and methods for TCGA abbreviations) had exceptionally high levels of mtRNAs, while samples from lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) expressed comparatively low levels of mtRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Samples from lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) expressed comparatively low levels of mtRNAs.
source: For example, compared to other tissues, samples derived from the kidney (TCGA studies KICH, KIRC, and KIRP, see Materials and methods for TCGA abbreviations) had exceptionally high levels of mtRNAs, while samples from lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) expressed comparatively low levels of mtRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is good agreement between mtRNA expression and MT protein levels with respect to their ordering across tissues.
source: When comparing our results to a prior study of MT protein abundances from the mouse (Pagliarini et al., 2008), we found good agreement between protein and mtRNA levels with respect to their ordering across tissues, (i.e. mtRNA expression and protein levels of MT-ND6 were highest in kidney, at moderate levels in liver, colon, and stomach, and lowest in lung).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data from Pagliarini et al., 2008.

claim: NUMTs are, in the vast majority of cases, integrated into intergenic/intronic regions of the nuclear genome, and are unlikely to be transcribed.
source: Previous work has shown that NUMTs are, in the vast majority of cases, integrated into intergenic/intronic regions of the nuclear genome, and are unlikely to be transcribed (Collura et al., 1996; Dayama et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collura et al., 1996 and Dayama et al., 2014.

claim: In the vast majority of samples, bona fide expression from mtDNA is 2–3 orders of magnitude greater than the expression of mtDNA pseudogenes.
source: In the vast majority of samples, bona fide expression from mtDNA is 2–3 orders of magnitude greater than the expression of mtDNA pseudogenes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The correlation between mtDNA copy number and mtRNA expression was highly tissue-type-specific.
source: We found that the correlation between mtDNA copy number and mtRNA expression was highly tissue-type-specific.
evidence: This is a summary of correlation analysis results.

claim: The data support a plausible correlation between mtDNA copy number and 'steady-state' mtRNA abundance across many but not all tissues.
source: Thus, the data support a plausible correlation between mtDNA copy number and 'steady-state' mtRNA abundance across many but not all tissues.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from correlation analysis.

claim: Correlations between mtDNA and mtRNA were not necessarily homogeneous between tumor and normal samples from the same tissue.
source: Interestingly, correlations between mtDNA and mtRNA were not necessarily homogeneous between tumor and normal samples from the same tissue.
evidence: This is an observation from correlation analysis, particularly in KICH.

claim: Several recent reports have described somatic changes to the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) in tumors.
source: Several recent reports have described somatic changes to the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) in tumors, which have expanded our knowledge of cancer genetics as well as basic mitochondrial biology (Davis et al., 2014; Joshi et al., 2015; Ju et al., 2014; Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davis et al., 2014; Joshi et al., 2015; Ju et al., 2014; Stewart et al., 2015.

claim: RNA-sequencing data was re-aligned from TCGA tumors to quantify mtDNA expression (mtRNA).
source: Here, we use orthogonal RNA-sequencing data to quantify mtDNA expression (mtRNA), and report analogously lower expression of mtRNA in tumors (relative to normal tissue) across a majority of cancer types.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Lower expression of mtRNA in tumors (relative to normal tissue) was observed across a majority of cancer types.
source: Here, we use orthogonal RNA-sequencing data to quantify mtDNA expression (mtRNA), and report analogously lower expression of mtRNA in tumors (relative to normal tissue) across a majority of cancer types.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Several cancers exhibit a trio of mutually consistent evidence suggesting a drop in respiratory activity: depletion of mtDNA copy number, decreases in mtRNA levels, and decreases in expression of nuDNA-encoded respiratory proteins.
source: Several cancers exhibit a trio of mutually consistent evidence suggesting a drop in respiratory activity: depletion of mtDNA copy number, decreases in mtRNA levels, and decreases in expression of nuDNA-encoded respiratory proteins.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple analyses in the study.

claim: A minority of cancer types exhibit a drop in mtDNA expression but an increase in nuDNA expression of respiratory proteins.
source: Intriguingly, a minority of cancer types exhibit a drop in mtDNA expression but an increase in nuDNA expression of respiratory proteins, with unknown implications for respiratory activity.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from differential expression analysis.

claim: The results indicate suppression of respiratory gene expression across many cancer types.
source: Our results indicate suppression of respiratory gene expression across many cancer types.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on multiple analyses.
